stem: In a total population cohort of 56 946 children born between 1 July 1990 and 31 December 1991 all those with a current clinical diagnosis of pervasive developmental disorder (n=255) or considered at risk of having the undetected disorder by virtue of having a statement of special educational needs (n=1515) were screened using the Social Communication Questionnaire (SCQ). A total of 1035 (return rate 58.5%) returned the SCQ and opted in for further assessments. Of these 1035, a stratifi ed subsample (n=255) received a comprehensive diagnostic assessment using ICD-10 research diagnostic criteria to derive a clinical consensus diagnosis of childhood autism, other autistic-spectrum disorders or no autistic-spectrum disorder. Further for 36 randomly selected children, eight internationally recognised experts using ICD-10 criteria compared project consensus diagnoses with their independent ICD-10 diagnoses. Agreement between the project consensus and expert diagnoses was 93% with (weighted) = 0.77. For the current study, parents of a subsample of children (n=119) completed both the SRS (Social Responsiveness Scale) and the Children's Communication Checklist (CCC) in addition to the SCQ. This aff orded an opportunity to directly compare the instrument properties of the three screens in the same sample. For this subsample of 119 children with data on all three screening instruments the mean age at SCQ screening was 10.2 years .The CCC was completed by parents immediately before the diagnostic assessment (mean age of children=12.0 years). The SRS was completed at a mean age of 12.6 years: for 50 children this was in advance of, and for 69 this was following, the diagnostic assessment and completion of the CCC. Scores on the three screening instruments were not consulted during the consensus clinical diagnostic process. The 119 children in this subsample diff ered from the remainder of the cohort that received detailed diagnoses (n=136) in terms of IQ (mean=78.5 in the included sample v. 67.4 in excluded sample P<0.001) but not symptom severity or parental education. Thirty-three children received a clinical consensus diagnosis of childhood autism; 37 a clinical consensus diagnosis of other autistic-spectrum disorders (other-ASD); and 49 children did not meet clinical consensus diagnosis for autism or other autistic-spectrum disorders (non-ASD). On examining the properties of the three instruments (SCQ, SRS and CCC) the following results were obtained: SCQ (cut off 15) had a sensitivity 0.86 and specifi city of 0.78. SRS (cut off 75) has a sensitivity of 0.78 and specifi city of 0.67. CCC (cut off 132) had a sensitivity of 0.93 and specifi city of 0.46. Ref: Charman, T., Baird, G., Simonoff , E., Loucas, T., Chandler, S., Meldrum, D., & Pickles, A. (2007). Effi cacy of three screening instruments in the identifi cation of autistic-spectrum disorders. The British Journal of Psychiatry, 191(6), 554-559. If you want to choose the best screening tool for assessment of autistic spectrum disorders among children attending special needs schools, which of the following factors will preclude using the results of the above study?
options: Using international psychiatric experts for gold standard diagnosis
Poor agreement between the international experts and the consensus group
Absence of blinded gold standard diagnosis
The age of the screened sample
correctAnswer: The age of the screened sample
reference:
Charman, T., Baird, G., Simonoff , E., Loucas, T., Chandler, S., Meldrum, D., & Pickles, A. (2007). Effi cacy of three screening instruments in the identifi cation of autistic-spectrum disorders. The British Journal of Psychiatry, 191(6), 554-559. If you want to choose the best screening tool for assessment of autistic spectrum disorders among children attending special needs schools, which of the following factors will preclude using the results of the above study?

stem: Antipsychotic Drugs and Hyperglycemia in Older Patients With Diabetes Background: Evidence suggests that there is an association between antipsychotic drugs and new-onset diabetes, but little is known about the risk of hyperglycaemia among persons with pre-existing diabetes. Methods: Using population-based health databases in Ontario, Canada, persons aged 66 years or older with diabetes who started treatment with an antipsychotic drug from April 1, 2002, to March 31, 2006, were followed up from treatment start until March 31, 2007. The cohort was subdivided into 3 groups: insulin-treated, an oral hypoglycaemic agent only -treated, and no diabetes treatment. We defi ned cases as patients hospitalized (emergency department visit or hospital admissions) for hyperglycaemia. Each case was matched with up to 10 controls for age, sex, year of cohort entry and duration of follow-up. The authors compared the likelihood of hyperglycaemia among current users of atypical and typical antipsychotic agents with that among remote antipsychotic users (discontinued >180 days), based on prescriptions closest to the event date. Results: Of 13 817 patients studied, 1515 (11.0%) were hospitalized for hyperglycaemia. Current antipsychotic treatment was associated with a higher risk of hyperglycaemia compared with remote antipsychotic use in all diabetes treatment groups (overall adjusted rate ratio, 1.50; 95% confi dence interval, 1.29-1.74). The risk was increased among patients who were treated with atypical and typical antipsychotic agents and was extremely high among patients who were just starting treatment (only 1 prescription before event). Conclusions: Among older patients with diabetes, the initiation of treatment with antipsychotic drugs was associated with a signifi cantly increased risk of hospitalization for hyperglycaemia (P < .001). The risk was particularly high during the initial course of treatment and was increased with the use of all antipsychotic agents. Ref: Lipscombe et al., Arch Intern Med. 2009;169(14):1282-1289 Of 13 817 patients studied, 1515 (11.0%) were hospitalized for hyperglycaemia. This 11% refers to

Baseline risk of hyperglycaemia in diabetic patients older than age 66, not taking antipsychotics
Baseline risk of hyperglycaemia in non-diabetic patients older than age 66
correctAnswer: Baseline risk of hyperglycaemia in the diabetic patients older than age 66 and treated with antipsychotics
explanation: The number 13817 includes all subjects in this study (both cases and controls) who belong to the cohort of diabetic, elderly patients, who received an antipsychotic prescription.

explanation: The minimization method was described by Taves and Pocock and Simon. Taves' article coined the term "minimization." stem: In the hierarchy of evidence based medicine, the grade conferred to expert consensus statements is
explanation: The hierarchy of evidence based on the Oxford Centre for Evidence-based Medicine Levels of Evidence is as follows: I Evidence obtained from a systematic review of all relevant randomised control trials. II Evidence obtained from at least one properly designed randomised control trial. III-1 Evidence obtained from well-designed pseudo-randomised controlled trials (alternative allocation or some other method). III-2 Evidence obtained from comparative studies (including systematic reviews of such studies) with concurrent controls and allocation not randomised, cohort studies, case-control studies, or interrupted time series with a control group. III-3 Evidence obtained from comparative studies with historical control, two or more single-arm studies, or interrupted time series without a parallel control group. IV Evidence obtained from case-series, either post-test or pre-test and post-test. V Expert opinion without a critical appraisal, or based on physiology, bench research, or historically based clinical principles.

This provided safety data and also a trend to a better outcome in post-myocardial infarction patients who were randomized to treatment with sertraline compared with placebo, but there was little diff erence in depression status between groups receiving sertraline and placebo after 24 weeks of treatment. However, the eff ect of sertraline was greater in the patients with severe and recurrent depression. In a smaller study (n=81) comparing paroxetine and nortriptyline (a TCA) both treatments were similarly eff ective in reducing depressive symptoms, but paroxetine was better tolerated than nortriptyline and less likely to produce cardiovascular side eff ects. The Myocardial Infarction and Depression-Intervention Trial (MIND-IT) evaluated mirtazapine (and citalopram second line) in post MI depression. But an active treatment strategy for depression post-myocardial infarction did not improve the long-term depression status or cardiac prognosis compared with usual care. van Melle, J.P., de jonge, P., Honig, A., et al (2007) Eff ects of antidepressant treatment on long-term depression status and cardiac prognosis in depressed MI patients. correctAnswer: You ask psychologists and social workers who provide care to the participating patients to be the study subjects to achieve a wider perspective → Purposive sampling, You include an independent rater to look at the data collected when analysing it. → Triangulation, You want a systematic approach of analysing the data alongside the collection. → Grounded theory, Method used to reach adequate sample size → Theoretical saturation
explanation:
To reach adequate sample size and stop collecting data, the point of theoretical saturation is employed in qualitative research. The data is iteratively analysed and at the point where no more new categories emerge, the data collection ceases. This point is called as theoretical saturation. Triangulation compares the results from either two or more diff erent methods of data collection or two or more data sources. The researcher looks for patterns of convergence to develop or corroborate an overall interpretation. In investigator triangulation, more than one investigator is involved, andfi ndings are cross-validated. Purposive sampling is one of the most common sampling strategies in qualitative research. (Note that snowball sampling and quota sampling are also used often). In purposive sampling the participants are selected according to a preselected criteria relevant to a particular research question - hence it is not random. Sample sizes, which may or may not befi xed prior to data collection, depend on the resources

and time available, as well as the study's objectives. Purposive sample sizes are often determined on the basis of theoretical saturation (the point in data collection when new data no longer bring additional insights to the research questions). Purposive sampling is, therefore, most successful when data review and analysis are done in conjunction with data collection. Grounded theory refers to constant comparison of the collected data alongside the data collection (iterative analysis)

Case 1 is General Paresis of insane, an impairment of mental function caused by damage to the brain from untreated tertiary syphilis. The psychiatric symptoms include hallucinations and delusions (especially grandiosity), mood changes (euphoria and mania), and changes in one's personality and speech. The physical symptoms include brief, sharp, "lightning" pains that occur with tabes dorsalis, eye changes and abnormal pupil response and overactive refl exes. In humans, the disease aff ects mainly young men in 20s-40s with cerebellar ataxia and myoclonus being prominent; the typical course is 1-2 yrs until death.

Case 3 is Normal pressure hydrocephalus. NPH is a syndrome where there is dilatation of cerebral ventricles (especially the third ventricle) and normal CSF pressure at lumbar puncture. It typically presents with the triad of dementia, gait ataxia, and urinary incontinence. The diagnosis rests on clinical suspicion. Disturbance of balance and gait is the cardinal feature and patients walk with a mildly broad-based, short stepped gait, which is also symmetrical.
